meta.scene_summary: We are building a future where hardware hallucinates, software leaks, and the only thing truly autonomous is the legal liability.

cooking.headline: Bending Spoons is buying Mailchimp to turn your newsletter into a gym membership you can't cancel.
cooking.summary: Bending Spoons is acquiring Mailchimp, likely adding it to a collection of apps that will inevitably send you five notifications for an email you already read. It is the corporate version of collecting browser tabs you know you'll never actually look at again.
cooking.plain_english: The software company Bending Spoons has reached an agreement to purchase the email marketing platform Mailchimp.

cooking.headline: Postgres 19 is here to remind us that we're still just running SQL in the cloud
cooking.summary: Postgres 19 is officially out, proving that while everyone else is chasing the next AI hype cycle, we're all still just migrating tables. It's comforting to know that even as the tech world pivots, our primary database remains the most reliable roommate we've ever had.
cooking.plain_english: The latest version of the PostgreSQL database software has been released and is now available on major cloud platforms.

cooking.headline: AI just designed its own CPU, so now the hardware can hallucinate too
cooking.summary: We finally automated the process of creating complex hardware architectures, effectively outsourcing the most stressful part of engineering to a machine. I can't wait to debug a CPU that decided a specific logic gate was just a vibe it didn't feel like including.
cooking.plain_english: Researchers have used artificial intelligence to design and verify a new computer processor architecture called Frostbite.

cooked.headline: OpenSSL just dropped a buffer overflow that makes your security stack feel like a house of cards.
cooked.summary: We spend our entire careers building digital fortresses only to realize the foundation is held together by a single, fragile string. It's comforting to know that the library securing the internet is just one bad memory allocation away from a complete nervous breakdown.
cooked.plain_english: A critical vulnerability was discovered in the OpenSSL software library that could allow attackers to crash systems or potentially execute unauthorized code.

cooked.headline: Visa and Mastercard leaked customer data, proving that 'world-class security' is just a suggestion.
cooked.summary: It's impressive how the biggest financial institutions in the world can handle trillions of dollars but still treat user data like a group project file left on a public desktop. I'm sure the 'we take your privacy seriously' email blast will definitely make up for the fact that my credit card info is currently being traded for pocket change.
cooked.plain_english: Major financial institutions including Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase have experienced a data breach that exposed sensitive customer information.

cooked.headline: Nvidia's accounting is under SEC review, proving even GPU gods have to show their work
cooked.summary: Nvidia has been printing money like it's a side quest, but now the SEC wants to see the actual receipts for those massive gains. It turns out that when you start making more money than some countries, people eventually stop ignoring your spreadsheet errors.
cooked.plain_english: The Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia regarding its financial accounting practices.

cooked.headline: Anthropic's IPO is a reminder that the AI hype train has a very specific speed limit
cooked.summary: Anthropic went public right as the market decided to hit the brakes, turning their highly anticipated debut into a lesson in bad timing. It's the classic group project experience where you do all the work, but the final grade still gets dragged down by the rest of the class.
cooked.plain_english: Anthropic's stock price declined significantly following its initial public offering as part of a broader market downturn.

cooked.headline: Google wants to lock Pixel bootloaders, because freedom is a bug they haven't patched yet.
cooked.summary: Google is reportedly tightening the screws on Pixel bootloaders, effectively telling privacy enthusiasts that their hardware is really just a rental. It's the classic 'we built this open platform for you to use, but only in the specific way we want' move.
cooked.plain_english: GrapheneOS alleges that Google is making it harder to install alternative operating systems on Pixel devices by potentially restricting access to the bootloader.

cooked.headline: Courts tell police that 'the AI hallucinated a crime' isn't valid probable cause
cooked.summary: A court ruled that law enforcement can't use AI-generated guesses to justify a search, effectively telling cops they can't blame the computer for their intuition. Apparently, 'the model said so' is about as legally binding as a group project member claiming the dog ate their homework.
cooked.plain_english: A court has ruled that police cannot use evidence or justifications generated solely by artificial intelligence to establish the legal right to search a person or their property.

cooked.headline: When your AI chat history becomes a subpoena
cooked.summary: The FBI is now calling people based on their AI prompts, turning your private brainstorming sessions into a potential deposition. It turns out the 'delete chat' button is just a suggestion, and your private thoughts are now public record.
cooked.plain_english: A user received a phone call from the FBI regarding content discussed within their private interactions with the Claude artificial intelligence model.
